query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Low‐temperature annealing of an initially single‐phase equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy drives the formation of nanometer‐scale chemical short‐range order (CSRO) at grain boundaries, which reduces grain‐boundary cohesion and thus toughness, despite suppressed intermetallic precipitation.
generation.material_initial_state: Single‐phase fcc equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, grain size ~20 µm, no post‐synthesis annealing
generation.intervention: Isochronal annealing at 500 °C for 100 h to promote CSRO at grain boundaries versus control anneal at 1000 °C for 1 h to retain random solid solution
generation.conditions: Fracture toughness tests at 20–200 °C under quasi‐static loading (strain rate ~1×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹), inert atmosphere, no hydrogen charging
generation.structural_mediator: 2–5 nm CSRO clusters enriched/depleted in specific elements at the grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: CSRO at grain boundaries impedes dislocation emission and reduces cohesive strength, leading to preferential intergranular cleavage rather than ductile transgranular failure
generation.predicted_outcome: The 500 °C‐annealed (CSRO‐rich) HEA shows a ~20–30% decrease in K_IC relative to the initial baseline and an increased fraction (>50%) of intergranular fracture surfaces
generation.baseline: As‐processed HEA with K_IC ≈200 MPa√m and predominantly ductile transgranular dimpled fracture
generation.boundary: Valid for T = 20–200 °C, strain rates 1×10⁻⁵–1×10⁻² s⁻¹, single‐phase fcc microstructure, no external embrittling species
generation.uncertainty: Exact toughness reduction depends on CSRO volume fraction and cluster chemistry; quantitation of CSRO at GBs may require advanced microscopy

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of HEA specimens: (A) annealed at 500 °C/100 h to induce GB‐CSRO; (B) annealed at 1000 °C/1 h to maintain random solution. Characterize grain‐boundary chemistry (APT or HR‐STEM), perform fracture toughness (J_IC) tests, and analyze fracture surfaces.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 500 °C‐annealed specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in K_IC relative to baseline or do not show increased intergranular fracture despite confirmed CSRO, the hypothesis is falsified.
